comments.body:
I ended up just taking the raw row and manually doing the transformation without any dapper constructs. I don't have any plans to revisit this for the time being. Probably isn't really worth the time.

Even so, am I correct that this behavior appears to be a bug?

No it's not a bug. It's more that you're not using the `TypeHandler` correctly.

Not sure what you expected and your sample shows some inconsistencies so it's hard to see what you expect exactly e.g. you did not provide any definition for `ItemJsonSchema` nor `DialtoneTemplateJsonSchema`.

As @andy-g said, the `SqlMapper.TypeHandler` is to handle **one** type of property so it will handle only **one** value of the result row.

In this example, if your property is typed `String[]` and your database field is typed `String`, the standard deserialization to `Item` class will fail because of that field: it does not know how to make a `String[]` from a `String`.

That's where `SqlMapper.TypeHandler<T>` comes into play.  
The `Parse` method defines how, from a database value, we turn it into a value of type `T`.  

In your case, a `TypeHandler<string[]>` will define how to turn a database value, passed as `object value` but actually of type `String`, into a `String[]`.

Here's a few detailed examples for your case:
- [by default](https://github.com/doc212/dapper-issue-929/blob/v0-exception/Program.cs) the `Query` method fails with an invalid cast exception from `String` to `String[]` for the `Keywords` property
- [with a string array type handler](https://github.com/doc212/dapper-issue-929/blob/v1-string-array/Program.cs) we have defined how we want to turn a `string` into a `string[]`.  
The potential problem with this implementation is that the defined `TypeHandler` will always be used to handle properties of type `String[]`.  
Say you have one field that represents arrays as comma separated and another field that uses space separated.  
You'd need 2 different implementations of the `String[] Parse(object value)` method but the problem is, only 1 `TypeHandler<String[]>` can be registered.
- [with an explicit KeywordsList type](https://github.com/doc212/dapper-issue-929/blob/v2-explicit-type/Program.cs) you overcome this limitation. Instead of typing your property `String[] Keywords` you type it `KeywordsList Keywords` and you can define a `TypeHandler<KeywordsList>` that will only kick in when a property of type `KeywordsList` is involved (which is basically a `string[]`)

Hope this helps.

title: CommandTimeout does not cause exception when exceeded

comments.body:
Dapper does not concatenate commands, and cannot do so: most providers have
a maximum parameter count that is prohibitive. And frankly - Dapper doesn't
want to be involved in large-scale SQL rewriting. For this to be a
like-for-like comparison of Dapper, your baseline test should be:

- loop over the Enumerable.Range
- execute a command object once per item via a sqlite command object

What you are most likely seeing is round-trip time: latency. Now, there are
sometimes vendor-specific ways around that. For example, on SQL Server, we
could talk about SqlBulkCopy, or we could talk about "MARS" and overlapped
pipelined commands. But I don't think those exist for sqlite.

There is one other possibility here, which is that we're talking about
mandatory prepared statements and the prepare overhead. To check that, a
comparison baseline loop should create a single parameterized query, call
Prepare on or once, the run the loop that sets the parameter values and
calls ExecuteNonQuery each time. Now: if *that* timing is significantly
better than Dapper, then *in that scenario* there is a potential change
that Dapper could make to improve things. In fact, I'd be genuinely
interested in the results of that test. It all comes down to mandatory vs
optional command preparation. This is a topic I have discussed here
http://blog.marcgravell.com/2017/12/dapper-prepared-statements-and-car-tyres.html
- it also hints at the change we could potentially make in Dapper for this
specific scenario - the enumerable arg to Execute.

(edit: removed footer junk that was left by email reply)

Some additional context here: sqlite has aggressive transaction semantics that can impact the performance of lots of inserts; according to http://www.sqlite.org/faq.html#q19 you might improve the performance if you create an explicit transaction and pass that transaction into all of the calls

Thanks @JaseRandall  - I suspected that would make a big difference, but since I'm not a sqlite expert I had to rely on anecdotal evidence. With this update, @DumpsterDoofus, I'm going to consider this "closed", since it seems clear that this is a sqlite feature with a simple workaround. If you disagree, please let me know and we can reopen.

totally miss errors.

comments.body:
It isn't clear to me whether the issue is the *width* (the content per-row) or the *height* (number of rows). If some of those columns are actually huge strings or blobs, then note that SSMS *doesn't actually fetch all the contents* - it has configurable options on the maximum column width to retrieve, so: if the issue is *width*, then your SSMS comparison *might be be comparing what you think it is comparing*. If each row actually has huge text/binary payloads, then : you're fundamentally going to be using a lot of memory.

If the issue is *height*, then note that by default dapper pre-loads all your data into a `List<T>` for convenience. This is fine in most cases and avoids a lot of complexity; as a side note, you might prefer to use `.AsList()` instead of `.ToList()` which will avoid a double-allocation of the list (actually: do that first, see if it fixes it!).

However! For very tall results you might prefer to iterate directly over the open reader. The tricky thing, however, is remembering that your command is *still open* while you `foreach` over it in this case, so don't do anything like close the connection or issue another command on the same connection *until you have finished* the `foreach`. To enable this mode, simply add the optional `buffered: false` parameter to dapper's `Query...` method.

Note that the `buffered: false` approach can *also* help improve things when *width* is the problem - since you would be iterating over each row in turn, *previous* rows (and their large payloads) will presumably be collectable by the GC.

@mgravell  Changing to `?foo?` works. But `@foo` always gives me  a "fixed" inside order without respect to the sqlstatements,resulting in a mispositioned INSERT or even a type mismatch error.  
What's wrong with `@`?

Dapper assumes that the db provider it is using isn't being stupid and
assumes that if the provider offers named parameter support, the provider
knows how named parameters work. It turns out that the accrss provider
doesn't meet this low bar. Basically, given the following:

command text = "select @foo, @bar"

add param "bar" with value 123

add param "foo" with value 456

Then what the access driver does is:

command text = "select ?, ?"

add param with value 123

add param with value 456

---

This erasure of all names obviously has the effect of reversing the
intended parameter order, so it is incredibly dependent on the parameters
being added in a specific order. This is not normal for named parameters,
and dapper doesn't attempt to force any specific order on the parameters.

IMO what the access driver should have done is - if it detects named
parameters: add the parameters to the underlying connection *in the order
in which they originally appeared in the query*. However this is very
unlikely to be fixed in the access driver.

The other thing we could potentially do is make dapper add parameters in
the order defined by the position of that named token in the query. Perhaps
not unreasonable, just... usually unnecessary.

Similar to #894, without an example or use case (we've only seen 1 request for this) and no follow-up, this isn't something we can chase down. If someone has examples/use cases for this, I'll re-open this for discussion!
@NickCraver As requested, a use case with ADO.NET examples has been provided. I have a similar use case in several different products. Please re-open this feature request.

The main problem here, though, is lifetime, especially when reading data *from* the database; you still need to access the data sequentially here, IIRC, including both row-wise and column-wise, which makes it very hard to expose in a direct API - unless it is "single column, non-buffered rows". Perhaps one viable option is some kind of leased memory construct (perhaps tying into non-contiguous buffers). It is something that needs quite a lot of thought, is the biggest thing.
There's probably a major use case where you read the stream for a single record.  What do you mean by lifetime?  Lifetime of what?

by the lifetime here, I'm talking about the timing of how/when we provide the caller with a row of data, and what has been populated at that point; we can't read columns past the stream, IIRC (it has been a while since I tried, admittedly) - and we can't change row - without breaking the stream. This puts *lots* of limitations on the usual expectations that folks have. Frankly, I wonder whether the pragmatic thing here is for this to be a use of the `ExecuteReader` API (pretty sure we have that now), i.e. let Dapper deal with the command prep and exec, and let the consumer deal with the reader (i.e. *they* call `GetStream`). In fact, I *believe* the example you provide is broken - it disposes the stream before you've read anything from it, which means it will almost certainly break.

Has something like SQL Server reader.GetStream(columnIndex) been implemented in Dapper yet?  This post is quite old.

I converted my code to native .NET SQL in the 2 cases where I needed to interact with a large varbinary.  The performance boost was exceptional. However, I hate to switch in and out of different frameworks in code. I prefer the Dapper style and its productivity gains.

@jeffreywstevens the problem with that is scoping and making sure the stream is valid when you want to use it; unless we implement some kind of callback API, we will have changed column, changed row, and/or closed the reader entirely - all before you even get to play with it. I'm happy to consider options but the tricky bit is coming up with a usage scenario that would be valid, without needing to buffer everything in advance. It kinda feels like a scenario where we'd want the caller to supply a `Func<Stream, Task>` so we can get the scoping right.

I did something similar to what is suggested but followed something closer to EF's "Timestamp" approach for optimistic locking and added it to Dapper Contrib.

If a dapper object has a property with a [Timestamp] attribute, my modified dapper update method ensures the timestamps match and issues a new one when updating.

The result is essentially:
```sql
UPDATE {Table} SET {normal dapper set pairs}, {TimestampProperty} = {NewTimestamp} WHERE Id = {Id} AND {TimestampProperty} = {OldTimestamp}
```

The benefit of this approach is not having to keep a clone of the original. The downside is it does require  database changes (a timestamp).

@ftedin This just isn't in the goals of Dapper, you're looking for a more "full blown" ORM. The goals of Dapper are to be simple and fast. Full change tracking is something other providers like EF Core are here to tackle. I'm going to close this out because we do acknowledge the feature request, but it's not something we would add to the core project.

what are the relative sizes of the different grids here? Is the second one
very wide (lots of columns), very tall (lots of rows), or does it have
large payloads (huge strings or byte arrays in cells)?

What you have looks fine. You could change ToList to AsList, but that's
about it. I suspect that this is a bandwidth issue from one of the above
issues.

Note that for excessively tall grids it may be useful to read it
unbuffered, but that will only help if you consume it via foreach
immediately. It won't help if you just read it unbuffered and shove it into
a list. The point of unbuffered is to allow you to process items as they
come in, overlapping IO and processing, and reduce the perceived latency of
the first row. If you aren't going to process it while it is arriving, it
won't help.

comments.body:
A few counter-points:
- Wouldn't having 2 of every query method be an even worse design choice? We already have to have many dozens of them for the overloads. 
- I disagree that a `List<T>` being buffered is obvious to *most* developers. Given `List<T>` is `IEnumerable<T>`, we're simply using the most common abstraction type.
- There's a `.AsList()` extension method for a performance optimized path for both

I don't see us changing this in v2, since adding a duplicate method for the minority use case isn't without adding confusion and double maintenance in itself.

> I disagree that a List<T> being buffered is obvious to most developers.

@NickCraver  That would surprise me a lot. For most people and in most programming languages a collection is fully evaluated and accessible as soon as it is created. Lazyness is what is usually unexpected. IEnumerable is the typical abstraction you use in c# to express the fact "you cannot be sure items exist before you ask for them.". This is why most tools are warning you when you're trying to evaluate an enumerable twice.

> Given List<T> is IEnumerable<T>, we're simply using the most common abstraction type.

As a general principle of programming one should try to provide the most specific type they can. Plenty of methods in Dapper and elsewhere could be merged into a single one by returning any common supertype you want with the actual underlying type dependent on the value of additional parameters. Would this be simpler? I don't think so. In this case you would not be able to express the fact that you **know** the result is in fact more specific that what the type system can tell you. Basically the pattern you're using here is **defeating** the type system.

> As a general principle of programming one should try to provide the most specific type they can.

We are. `IEnumerable<T>` is the most common denominator. With 1 complaint about this being confusing and millions of users, I'm not really sure what the goal is here. To be frank: we will not be doubling the surface area of the library. You'd be talking about many dozens of duplicate methods for questionable benefit. I'm sorry you find the behavior questionable, but it's not something we're going to change or break a ton of people's code for. Sometimes people disagree on design decisions, and that's okay.

title: Read(buffered=true) is a questionable design choice

comments.body:
Are you enabling MARS in the connection string in this example? If not, this isn't something supported by ADO.NET itself. In any case, you need to do 2 things for this code (a situation in which you have *multiple concurrent results being fetched*):
1. MARS enabled on the connection string.
2. You need to open and close the connection around it.

Dapper supports opening and closing the connection itself (closing what it opened) on both sync and async APIs, but not when you have ***multiple concurrent*** async calls on the same connection (again: only supported by MARS).

We can't really detect this state without adding a ton of ref and activity counting (and the activity *may not be from Dapper*) on each connection. So: there's not much we can do. The thinking is: if you're using MARS and multiple concurrent `async` SQL calls: you know what you're doing, and the limits. And you probably *don't* want Dapper managing the connection, since you're trying to squeeze every ounce of performance out of complete control.

Thanks for your update, actually the problem comes from a bad use of async.

I hit the problem again, I have MARS enabled and I manually open the connection.

If I have two or three queries it's fine, but if I have a lot more queries then I have this exception.

I think that too many async queries on an Azure Database is not the best thing to do, I'll have to dig a bit on how to manage a lot of async queries to avoid this exception.

I wasn't aware this was added to EF Core in 2.0. I strongly object to such a feature. Here's a demo project showing just some of the ways it can be done incorrectly and not actually parameterized: https://github.com/NickCraver/EFCoreInjectionSample/blob/master/Program.cs

I'm raising these issues with the EF team now. I wish I had seen this before the 2.0 release, I sincerely hope it gets deprecated and removed ASAP. If they took *only* a `FormattableString`, it'd have almost none of the worries, but it doesn't. They implement it with [implicit operations on a struct](https://github.com/aspnet/EntityFrameworkCore/blob/44119b3962513adc20b98a53567b968644904360/src/EFCore.Relational/RawSqlString.cs) which adds a lot of danger as developers can pass in strings that aren't being parameterized at all.

In Dapper, I don't think this is a good idea. An ORM that's no direct SQL *expect* a `FormattableString` (like EF could be) I totally see. For Dapper, I think it's firmly a net loss in perceived vs. actual security and the bugs it'd create.

I'm happy to discuss this at length, but as of now: I'm firmly against adding this. SQL injection is a serious issue, and we shouldn't add more ways and examples of how to screw that up.

indeed, it is already perfectly possible to screw up here by using dapper
with interpreted syntax incorrectly - but at least that's entirely in the
hands of the caller. In many ways, offering this feature even in different
named methods starts getting into the territory where the API *actively
leads people* into making an injection mistake, and that is definitely
worth avoiding at all costs.

If we had done FormattableString only from the start, then it'd have far fewer issues, but can't really do so now.
I'm sorry, I know nothing about this project. I was just talking generally about how they did it in EF Core.

There's other ways to disambiguate the method call.

1) using a named parameter, where the call would look like this: QueryFirst(formattable: $"...") - but this seems really fragile, and I don't think people would realize that a single named parameter can even affect overload resolution like this
2) using a method that would wrap a formattable string into a struct: QueryFirst(Parametrize($"...")) - here it's more obvious that something special is happening, but still nothing would prevent people from omitting the method call. On the other hand, nothing prevents people from doing that right now anyway, and Parametrize sounds really specific about what it's doing. First I thought about an extension method but that doesn't seem to work. Or no method at all - that struct could have a better name and be created explicitly.

But of course the best (and maybe the only acceptable) option would have been to make this the default and making Raw explicit - that way there would be no danger when accidentally omitting something.

Edit: Actually some of the danger when forgetting to make Parametrize explicit could be avoided the way they did it in EF Core - the default overload would be changed to take a new struct that supports implicit conversions from both - but throws when being created from a FormattableString (a breaking change - but who would honestly do that today? This still isn't completely perfect because you could always just create a temporary variable on a separate line as a string - even when using var, which wouldn't protect you when you forgot to make it explicit and just get cast to the struct from a string. comments.body: Do you have example code? We need some context here. There's a lot of questions which the code would clear up quickly.

ok, so using the query
```
SELECT * FROM ChatMessage WHERE GroupId = @GroupId
```
the above works if ```@GroupId``` is anything but NULL. If in C# we say ``` new { GroupID = null }```, Dapper does not change the query to say ```... WHERE GroupId IS NULL```.

The ```IS``` keyword being the important one. If it's left as ```WHERE GroupId = NULL``` then sql does not allow that.

The IS keyboard is an important one on *some* SQL languages. Behavior differs, so Dapper doesn't do anything special here. If you want to handle the null or not case, you'll want to change the query text to go along with it. This would be dangerous to handle in Dapper and break across providers.

It'd definitely be a breaking change of any sort regardless, so the recommendation is: switch your statement for the null case.

Ah I see - Ok thanks - I spent a while looking for some comment on this but there does not seem to be any, and I know dapper uses the ```x IN ()``` expression as a special one so I thought it might do the same for other variables.
In SQL Server you can SET ANSI_NULLS OFF to mitigate this issue.
Friends don't let friends use `SET ANSI_NULLS OFF`

Oh, according to https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/database-engine/deprecated-database-engine-features-in-sql-server-2017?view=sql-server-ver15 this feature is deprecated which I didn't realize because https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/statements/set-ansi-nulls-transact-sql?view=sql-server-ver15 does not mention it at all. Thanks for the warning! :)
I must say this issue is the single thing I don't like about dapper. Catches me out every single time. Seems if certain SQL statements are changed (like IN statements) then this one should be too.

Changing a connection level configuration option is ... brittle and dangerous. In this case there is already a semantic that perfectly encapsulates the logic you are trying to convey: "is null". Maybe I'm a purist, but IMO: use that, for that reason.

IMO "in" is different here, because there *isn't* a good semantic to express that in the generalized input case.

I guess to me it's the break in semantics of object property to sql param conversion. With the results in normal ADO.NET you get a DBNull value and that is cleanly converted to a Nullable<T>, while the opposite side of the equation (sending params to the query) means that if a variable might have a null in it, you would need 2 different sql statements.

That's why I brought up the IN expression - you have cleanly abstracted that one away to use a single way from a c# list to sql, so the NULL comparison feels weird.

So to me it's not about SQL purity but about Dapper purity 😉 

[edit] Oh and I do totally understand this would be a breaking change and not at all easy to implement. Just discussing things here, not demanding anything.

To be clear: You're using `char(36)` in MySQL to store actual strings, not GUIDs, but when querying the data the columns are acting like they're GUIDs automatically?

Dapper is really just a lightweight wrapper around the base ADO.NET database drivers to make mapping and submitting queries easier, it leaves the actual low-level details to the driver. You can check that page to see what options work for you, although switching to `varchar` columns might be the easiest if the data is really just strings.

Thanks for the prompt response and giving me the benefit of the doubt on your questions.

@mgravell has the right of it, @NickCraver. The solution I'm proposing is to use the name of the `ConstructorInfo` parameters to identify where the column could **potentially** map to, rather than the order in which the parameter appears in the constructor. For sure, four strings should not match a bunch of integers regardless of their parameter names. You would still want each potential constructor parameter to go through the [other normal type checking](https://github.com/StackExchange/Dapper/blob/61e965eed900355e0dbd27771d6469248d798293/Dapper/DefaultTypeMap.cs#L96) (i.e. number of columns equals number of constructor parameters, parameter type matches column type, etc.) to validate that the potential mapping is valid.

Using the name for column to constructor parameter mapping isn't new to Dapper, as the `DefaultTypeMap` implementation does precisely that right now, first to validate the column names via `SqlMapper.ITypeMap.FindConstructor()` [here](https://github.com/StackExchange/Dapper/blob/61e965eed900355e0dbd27771d6469248d798293/Dapper/DefaultTypeMap.cs#L94), and second to fetch the `ParameterInfo` object on the identified `ConstructorInfo` via `SqlMapper.ITypeMap.GetConstructorParameter()` [here](https://github.com/StackExchange/Dapper/blob/61e965eed900355e0dbd27771d6469248d798293/Dapper/DefaultTypeMap.cs#L145).

It is important to note that these two checks are case-insensitive, so if you have two constructor parameters with the same names but in different cases (`foo` and `FOO`) this would fail because the same constructor parameter would get fetched twice (whichever one was first) in `DefaultTypeMap.GetConstructorParameter()` [here](https://github.com/StackExchange/Dapper/blob/61e965eed900355e0dbd27771d6469248d798293/Dapper/DefaultTypeMap.cs#L145). This means unique constructor parameter names, regardless of case, are already required with the `DefaultTypeMap` implementation.

To add more clarity, I did a quick rewrite of [the current `DefaultTypeMap.FindConstructor()`](https://github.com/StackExchange/Dapper/blob/61e965eed900355e0dbd27771d6469248d798293/Dapper/DefaultTypeMap.cs#L79) that shows how it would work [here](https://gist.github.com/carusology/0480bd5227498a847180f987022ac4d8). This isn't enough because `SqlMapper` still expects the order to match [here](https://github.com/StackExchange/Dapper/blob/61e965eed900355e0dbd27771d6469248d798293/Dapper/SqlMapper.cs#L3007), hence me writing this issue instead of simply making my own `SqlMapper.ITypeMap` implementation and going on with my day.

Let me answer the questions directly:

>For example, what if the constructor was 4 strings? How would you make any logical assumptions about ordering?

The names of the columns would be checked against the names of the constructor parameters.

>Unless I'm misunderstanding you're saying "it will fail" above when you really mean "it won't run the constructor that doesn't match", is that correct?

Kind of. I would argue the constructor _does_ match in principle, because it is obvious that `SELECT foo, bar FROM MyExample` matches the constructor `MyExample(String bar, Guid foo)` assuming the data stored in those columns map to those C# types. I am raising this issue because the current Dapper implementation is inconsistent with my more liberal interpretation of a "matching constructor."
Followup: how should `params` be handled?

Interesting edge case.

I believe that goes beyond the scope of this issue. From what I have read of Dapper's code, I do not believe `params` is currently supported (_maybe_ it is if you slap on `[ExplicitConstructor]`?), but it isn't necessary to support the type of names-based mapping for which I am advocating. Note that this belief is couched on my assumption that it is not possible for a SQL query to return an array as the value for a column. 

Anyway, if I was to implement it, I would trust the developer consuming it, and further relax the constructor mapping to support a `params`-based constructor. This could be done by expanding the sorting used to identify a constructor in `DefaultTypeMap.FindConstructor()`.

Currently, [Dapper sorts constructors in the following order](https://github.com/StackExchange/Dapper/blob/61e965eed900355e0dbd27771d6469248d798293/Dapper/DefaultTypeMap.cs#L82):

1. accessor (first public, then protected, then private)
2. number of parameters (more parameters to less parameters)

I would change this to go by the following order instead:

1. **presence of `params` (non-`params` first, `params` second)**
2. accessor (first public, then protected, then private)
3. number of parameters (more parameters to less parameters)

Then, for each of the `params` cases, I would check if it was possible for the data provided via the SQL query to fit into the constructor. So if the constructor signature looks liked this...

```cs
MyImmutable(String foo, Guid bar, params int[] values) { /* [ ... ] */ }
```
... I would expect it to be compatible with a query like this:

```sql
SELECT Bar, Foo, Bizz, Buzz FROM MyImmutable;

DESCRIBE MyImmutable;
+--------------+-------------------+------+-----+---------+-------+
| Field        | Type              | Null | Key | Default | Extra |
+--------------+-------------------+------+-----+---------+-------+
| Bar          | char(36)          | NO   |     | NULL    |       |
| Foo          | varchar(255)      | NO   |     | NULL    |       |
| Bizz         | int (11)          | NO   |     | NULL    |       |
| Buzz         | int (11)          | NO   |     | NULL    |       |
+--------------+-------------------+------+-----+---------+-------+
```

This means a constructor of `MyImmutable(params object[] values)` would match all queries, but it would only be used as a last resort.

---

By the way, I am more than happy to contribute to this change, though I think I would struggle mightily with the explicit IL updates. I have always used compiled expressions to create cached delegates instead ([like this](https://github.com/invio/Invio.Extensions.Reflection/blob/master/src/Invio.Extensions.Reflection/PropertyInfoExtensions.cs#L267)).
Thanks for all the work here @carusology - added to the v2 list to see if we can support it.
This issues is now almost 8 years old. Is this still a thing? Or was this abandoned somewhere down the line

My view here would be that this need is met more effectively in the [AOT pieces](https://aot.dapperlib.dev/gettingstarted); this supports custom constructors without any demands on parameter order, and allows `[ExplicitConstructor]` to control the preferred constructor (in the case of ambiguity).
Thanks @mgravell for the heads-up - I will give it a shot

comments.body:
The very related API here (that I think sucks) is `splitOn` in these multi-map scenarios, e.g. `splitOn: "Id, UserId"` (defaults to `splitOn: "Id"`). It's string based and error-prone. Many people get it wrong once you leave the realm of `Id` being your PK column (or in the query).  Some (IMO, bad) ideas:

- We could have an array as the arg, but people are likely to allocate that on every call, likely resulting in: `splitOn: new[] { nameof(Foo.Id), nameof(User.UserId) }`
- The Column/Table proposal in #722 could be used as the default. So instead of "Id" (still the default), it'd look for, effectively: `splitOn: $"{Foo.PrimaryKeyField},{Bar.PrimaryKeyField}"`
   - This would be determined by the [Column] attributes on those types (or the mapping function, if it handles PK recognition).
   - Con: obviously doesn't work well for multi-column PKs
   - Very "heavy" compared to a string 

While these are more "safe" than a string, they're also by-simplest-usage more expensive. It'd be fantastic if we can pull a trick with tuples or something else that doesn't allocate so much and could get some of the safety features overall. Anyone have any fancy ideas for what they'd like that parameter to look like?
The fluent API looks really nice. What would the return type of `Query(sql, args)` be in that example?

Now C#7 has a [syntactic sugary coating for tuples](https://blogs.msdn.microsoft.com/dotnet/2017/03/09/new-features-in-c-7-0/), it should look the same.

So a query would look like:

`var resultrow = conn.Query<(string, int, int)>("select aString, anInt, anotherInt from aTable").ToList();`

named items in the tuple would be specified in the tuple definition between the <>, or the default Item1, Item2 would be used otherwise.

I assume the compiler would do a lot of the work here if it knew where to see the tuple definition, but given functions that can now look like: `(string first, string middle, string last) LookupName(long id)` then the compiler happily handles this. 

It might be possible to dynamically create the tuple from the query, but that won;t help the compiler, so I'm quite happy to strongly type it as I would if I was returning a POCO class, but in the case where you are returning a row of all columns (eg select *) then having each item in the tuple defined as a dynamically defined object sounds OK. 

I don't like the idea of the fluent version - I want to call some SQL in 1 line of code and have some results back into a variable. Defining it in one place and then running the same SQL or defining the SQL in a string and passing it into multiple lines that all look the same doesn't feel right. I want the equivalent of "dapper, gimme data now" not setting up definitions, setting up control options, and then running the query. 

Simple and consistent is good, so using the same mechanism C#7 now provides should be the default way, surely?!

Important: tuple names are only passed *outwards*, not *inwards*. Generics
here is an inwards. So the names would be ignored and it would be purely
positional.

comments.body:
yeah, I've been doing some looking in this area - it is particularly vexing that we can't pass them *in* as parameters sensible, and there's no *good* ways of passing them *out* without - as you note - it introducing different rules over name vs positional lookup. I'm still playing with a few things here. I'm genuinely in two minds as to how best to proceed. The problem isn't in *implementing* it; the problem is a human one - it is in *not causing other people problems*, essentially not being an "enabler" for their issues. The ambiguity / change over name/position is a tricky one and isn't necessarily obvious.

Needs thought more than anything.

I think that, while it would be nice to be able to pass them _in_, the existing anonymous type trick works pretty well to make that not a high priority.

But unless you use the workaround mentioned [here](http://stackoverflow.com/a/30469302/1872399), you can't materialize into a strongly typed object (I'm not a fan of dynamic) without declaring a type, which litters the codebase with little types, each only used once. It  becomes even worse (in my opinion) if you define some kind of super-type which contains all properties you ever use, where each property is only filled in some queries. IMO there should be a 1:1 direct mapping between all properties and all sql results.

So I think that being unable to pass tuples _out_ is slightly more annoying.

----------------------

Regardless of future design decisions (I trust you fully in this regards), what would you think about adding some kind of safeguard, so that users which expect this to already work get feedback that it doesn't?

My thinking would be to throw an exception if the target type is a ValueTuple, but no properties are filled (the sql does not contain Item1, Item2, ItemN). Such cases are surely 100% invalid user expectations.

That way 

```C#
_con.Query<(int, int)>("select 1 as Item1, 2 as Item2");
```

continues to work, but

```C#
_con.Query<(int id, int value)>("select 1 as id, 2 as value");
```

will throw.

I personally don't like that because it really uglifies the SQL.

If value-tuple doesn't currently work, it makes it easier to allow
special-casing it as a positional type. I'll keep digging and thinking.

Attributes Vs Config...

I really think Dapper should only support 1 convention, even if there's a group of people who don't like Attributes or prefer attributes and don't like Config.

Dapper is a beautiful tiny lightweight ORM that does the bare minimum. Yes it needs some mapping to get around legacy and poorly named tables/columns in databases, and vice versa. But not at the sacrifice of bloating Dapper.

/my 2 cents

-----

I'm impartial to Attributes vs Config. As long as Dapper doesn't lose focus and become bloat.

I highly prefer config (not attributes) based setup because I may not own the class/model, the other big ones are conventions. Working with legacy schema (I can't change) where all the tables are prefixed like `tb_TableName` or the columns are `chrColumnName` 🤢 

I prefer my database identity columns to be in the form of `TableNameID`, and my c# classes as just `ID`. I would like the flexibility to setup a convention to map `ID` to `[ClassName]Id` and just reuse it for all of my queries and stored procs.

Thanks!

I hope that the Dapper is supported in two ways, and Attribute is simple and intuitive. But I think Dapper in complex scenes require enhanced Mapper function, especially in the one-to-many, many-to-many scenario, EF-like configuration method based on Lambda expression expression ability.

A suggestion for the Attributes vs Config discussion:

Go with the Config option, and supply an implementation (in `Dapper.Contrib`?) which would do attribute mapping.  That way by default Dapper would remain small, but if Attribute mapping is required, add a reference to `Dapper.Contrib`.  You could even supply a `.UseAttributeMapping` extension which would apply all of the `Func<Type...>` required in one go if needs be.

Personal bias is towards Config rather than Attributes, but I could live with either.  Config feels more flexible however.

+1 for @Pondidum. The Config is a must for the `Dapper` Core, the Attributes are for `Dapper.Contrib` only (optional). Since I use `Dapper.Contrib` I will use the Attributes - and I would like to have an option to change/enhance the Attributes by the Config.

Just a minor note: you should decide, what will happen, when `TableNameMapper`, `ColumnNameMapper` return `null` or empty string - either fall back to the default mappers or throw an exception.
@Gonkers another option there is a virtual method on the attribute and subclass to change default behavior; worth consideration

@nickcraver - For conn.Query<Users>("select ...", ...), is it possible to name the "tables" in the split? spliton: "commentid, followerid", splitto: "Comment, User". @NickCraver I don't think using Options as static is a good thing.

Examples:

- Storing customer data on one database and global application on another.
- Converting a server database to SQLite to be sent to mobile users.

@Gonkers Yep, if that style suits you then by all means. In terms of performance it's hard to do that without allocations and analysis overhead at many points along the way, so an awesome task for a separate library to tackle.

@xmedeko That brings a big dependency injection dependency ;) I'd definitely say not something that's in the goals of Dapper, IMO.

I'm using Dapper exclusively (for the moment) on .NET Core projects, and at least for one of those projects, I haven't decided between PostgreSQL and MSSQL for production--the semantics may be slightly different for each one.

So, my preference would be a configuration object (which may or may not utilize attributes if available) that I can instantiate and inject. IMHO, the configuration object should be responsible for falling back to the default behavior. This would, for example, make it child's play to obtain the default value and then optionally decorate it -- adding a table prefix, lowercasing, etc. -- or to "disable" a field so it isn't read.

Some minor thoughts:

- If the configuration responds with null/empty for a given property, Dapper should ignore the property.

- The configuration object may need access to the POCO, not just its type, to determine the correct field name.

- If Insert and Update are planned for the future (I'm using SimpleCRUD now, so I hope this is the case!), the interface for obtaining the table/field name should include a flag for the action at hand. For example, a dev may need to *read* from a view but *insert/update* against a table, or certain fields may be computed or otherwise managed in the background for reading but should not be part of an INSERT/UPDATE.

- 10+ years ago, I had my own .NET ORM that used attributes for the field name and a few other odds and ends (default value for null, max length for string fields, etc.). Back then there was a performance hit for enumerating the attributes, enough so that I believe I ended up caching them. Is that still an issue? (If so, the default configuration implementation could cache them. Maybe JSON.NET would be a good library to check to see if they've had to work around any perf issues with attributes.)

@richardtallent thanks for chiming in, follow-ups with some more context:
> If the configuration responds with null/empty for a given property, Dapper should ignore the property.

I'm not sure *exactly* how this will work in both directions, but yes - probably this behavior.

> The configuration object may need access to the POCO, not just its type, to determine the correct field name.

This won't be possible, Dapper only figures out these bits once and caches the (de)serializer, via writing IL. So it's not per-object...we can't do that in a performant way. This functionality is what makes Dapper so fast.

> If Insert and Update are planned for the future...

I think these will remain in .Contrib, and will be able to access fields, but differing view vs. table read/writes, etc. likely will never be a target use case. If it's something that works then great, but I think it'd be hard to justify complication for them.

> Back then there was a performance hit for enumerating the attributes

See point 2 above - this isn't a tremendous concern since we cache the deserializer (and we'd cache this mapping, mental note: clearing it on a `Func<>` set). We want it to be fast, but there is an overall limited impact given the nature of Dapper here. @mgravell also maintains [protobuf-net](https://github.com/mgravell/protobuf-net), which we can steal a few tricks from here.

This is a more nuanced one than you would think; historically, indeed Dapper has let the downstream provider choose the types that it returns. Most ADO.NET providers know how to identify and cast a GUID column from their data store. We are aware that some providers don't do this correctly. We investigated automatically casting between GUID and byte[] in the cases where it didn't happen, but then another problem came up: endianness. It turns out that different backend stores use different endianness to store GUIDs. This means that there is no reliable endianness choice that Dapper can choose or infer that will work correctly in all cases. Because of this I'm not happy for dapper to provide a probably-wrong conversion.

so: you'll either need to use a provider that understands guids, or use byte[] and perform your own conversion (checking the results)

I think I'll take a look at how EntityFrameworkCore handles it (as I'm migrating the codebase from EF to Dapper). I did a first test at changing the column type in `CREATE TABLE` from `UNIQUEIDENTIFIER` to `NVARCHAR(64)`, however the problem still remains.

There's no problem saving the models with the Guid property with Dapper, however Microsofts SQLite provider still converts the value to an octet-stream regardless of column type. The problem occurs when deserializing the value, as Dapper still gets back a `byte[]` even though the actual column type is `NVARCHAR`.

The simple solution would of course be to change all models to have a string Id and just initialize them with `Id = Guid.NewGuid().ToString()`, but how much fun would that be ;)

@tidyui, I had a quick look at how EF core does it because I need this feature too. This is what I can tell from the code ( I am not a EF Core expert so please correct me if I am wrong ) :
1. Unique identifiers with Guid type are mapped to sqlite 'BLOB' types, not 'TEXT'
2. To write the Guid to db, it needs to convert it to a x'some-hex-value' string value for the insert/update sql query. EF does the [mapping](https://github.com/aspnet/EntityFramework/blob/dev/src/EFCore.Sqlite.Core/Storage/Internal/SqliteTypeMapper.cs#L57) and then creates the [value](https://github.com/aspnet/EntityFramework/blob/f386095005e46ea3aa4d677e4439cdac113dbfb1/src/EFCore.Relational/Storage/RelationalSqlGenerationHelper.cs#L460) actually used for the projected sql query
3. To read the Guid, it uses this DbDataReader and this [mapping](https://github.com/aspnet/EntityFramework/blob/f386095005e46ea3aa4d677e4439cdac113dbfb1/src/EFCore.Relational/Storage/TypedRelationalValueBufferFactoryFactory.cs#L52) but honestly from there I am not sure how he does it and I don't see anything specific to read Guid for Sqlite.
4. Guid.ToByteArray() is [used](https://github.com/aspnet/EntityFramework/blob/dev/src/EFCore.Sqlite.Core/Storage/Internal/SqliteSqlGenerationHelper.cs#L88) for the convertion from Guid to byte[]

Not too sure where to go from there though. I might use byte[] and perform my own conversion as suggested by @mgravell .

Yeah, I actually just changed all my GUIDS to NVARCHAR(36). The result is the same, the id is never changed so there's no need for re-indexing and all Guid's were generated by the repositories anyway :)
I can't do that unfortunately. I have too many Guid around and has deep implications in my code AND my database. Guid as a string are stored in more bytes than it does for a blob !!

@ethanli83 my experience is that `TypeHandler` works with C# `Guid` when Dapper converts the db type to C# type:
```

```

But it doesn't work when using `Guid` as a parameter like this:
```

```

This is currently a blocker for me in MiniPofiler.Providers.Sqlite as well. I can't use Microsoft.Data.Sqlite cleanly. This relates to #227 as well, since that *would* work here with most providers. Perhaps we should take another look at using the `.Get____()` methods on ADO.NET (for Guid and others)?

@mgravell thoughts? I know of the problems with for example `.GetChar()`, but I'd imagine GetGuid is far more stable. If we special cased here as we do for GetChar(), we may be in a better place overall. I can give this a go with some tests soon as time allows.

We've talked to the EF team about this while on campus last time, the TL;DR is: it sucks. GUID support across providers is a bad situation. But there's no consensus about where to paper over it either. I'm personally of the opinion ADO.NET should be where this happens (e.g. in the `Get___()` methods), but can absolutely see it both ways. I know this is an old discussion but the slow code in the example given was almost certainly caused by passing a string parameter (NVARCHAR) to a query that's comparing the parameter value with the VARCHAR field "SomeOtherId". SQL Server really doesn't like this (especially if the table being queried is big).

In the fast code example (where the actual string is used in the query as a quoted value) it runs fast since the SomeOtherId='blah' comparison is comparing VARCHAR SomeOtherId with 'blah' (also a VARCHAR). As such, no casting is needed and the query runs much faster. I think I'm right in saying that SQL Server will cast the table data to NVARCHAR in the slow example, rather than the casting the constant used in the comparison (hence the query slows more and more as the table grows).

Just a quick note about nullable reference types with the current iteration of Dapper (v2.0.78).

Using Dapper in a project, and enabling nullable reference types in that project results in false negatives for the null value checking mechanism as implemented by Microsoft.

For example the method `QuerySingleorDefaultAsync<T>` has the return type `Task<T>`. In this case Microsoft inaccurately assumes that T is never null. This causes the nullable reference type checking mechanism to break down so it cannot be relied upon.

This is a known limitation of the nullable reference type checking when not every single library used has it enabled and configured properly. Doing so in Dapper v3 will obviously fix this.

@NightWatchman It's a little more subtle than that. C# tracks it as neither "never null" nor "maybe null" but a [third state](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/nullable-references#nullability-of-types), "null-oblivious," due to the method not being declared in a context that has nullability annotations enabled. The effect is the same as what you're saying, in that you won't be warned if you dereference.

comments.body: ![capture](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/8716784/21385109/3cd88f1c-c7a8-11e6-8ada-6f184398f359.JPG)

I see that you have `buffered` set to `false`. If you do this and immediately close and dispose the connection, you're doing so before the results are read. You have 2 choices here:
- Let Dapper buffer these internally for you (the default, `buffered: true`)
- Or consume the results yourself before closing and disposing of the connection.

The current code has the effect of shutting the door while the results are still walking in, so that'll almost always blow up. The only way it'll succeed is if the query was so far and the result set so small as to finish before the `.Close()` call gets hit.

Also note: Dapper will `.Open()` and `.Close()` the connection for you, you can simply remove these calls. But the dispose (from the `using`) itself is still an issue in your illustration.
